content: Vitamin A deficiency is a condition that is prevalent in developing countries but is rarely observed in developed nations. Each year, approximately 250,000 to 500,000 malnourished children in developing regions lose their vision due to a lack of vitamin A. One of the earliest clinical manifestations of vitamin A deficiency is night blindness. This deficiency contributes to blindness by causing extreme dryness of the cornea (xerophthalmia) and by inflicting damage on both the retina and the cornea. In addition to its impact on vision, vitamin A deficiency weakens the immune system, reducing the body’s ability to combat infections. In regions where children are not routinely immunized, infectious diseases such as measles exhibit significantly higher mortality rates. Dr. Alfred Sommer has highlighted that even mild or subclinical vitamin A deficiency poses serious risks. It can increase the likelihood of respiratory and diarrheal infections, impair growth rates, slow bone development, and reduce the chances of survival during severe illnesses. While dietary insufficiency is a primary cause of vitamin A deficiency, other factors can also contribute. For instance, iron deficiency can interfere with the body’s ability to absorb vitamin A. Excessive alcohol consumption can deplete vitamin A stores, and a liver that is under stress from alcohol may be more vulnerable to vitamin A toxicity. Individuals who consume large amounts of alcohol are advised to consult a healthcare professional before taking vitamin A supplements. Treatment for vitamin A deficiency is available in both oral and injectable forms, typically administered as vitamin A palmitate.
